Month-to-month contract customers churn at 42.7%, vs 2.8% for two-year contracts — the single strongest churn driver.
Fiber optic customers churn at 41.9%, substantially higher than DSL (19.0%), suggesting pricing or service-quality issues with the fiber product.
Customers paying via 'Electronic check' churn most (45.3%), indicating automatic payment methods correlate with stronger retention.
Senior citizens churn at 41.7% vs 23.6% for non-seniors — an under-served, higher-risk segment.
Customers without a partner churn at 33.0% compared with 19.7% for those with a partner.
Customers without dependents churn at 31.3%, more than double the rate of customers with dependents (15.4%).
New customers (0-1 year tenure) churn at 47.4%, the highest of any tenure group, while 5+ year customers churn at just 6.6% — loyalty compounds sharply after year one.
Paperless billing customers churn at 33.6% vs 16.3% for paper billing customers.
Among internet subscribers, those without Online Security churn at 41.8% vs 14.6% with it — a clear upsell/retention lever.
Lack of Tech Support correlates with a churn rate of 41.6% vs 15.2% for subscribers who have it.
Churn falls steadily as add-on services increase: 21.4% churn with 0 add-ons vs 5.3% with 6 add-ons — bundling drives stickiness.
The 'Very High' monthly-charge tier ($100+) shows a churn rate of 28.3%, the highest across all charge bands.
Churned customers pay $74.44/month on average vs $61.27 for retained customers — a $13.18 premium that isn't translating into loyalty.
Average tenure at churn is just 18.0 months vs 37.6 months for retained customers, reinforcing that the first year is the critical retention window.
Total monthly recurring revenue at risk from already-churned customers is $139,130.85/month ($1,669,570.20 annualized).
Gender shows negligible impact on churn (26.2% Male vs 26.9% Female) — not a useful targeting variable.
Phone service subscribers churn at 26.7% vs 24.9% for non-subscribers, a modest difference.
Customers with multiple phone lines churn at 28.6% compared to 25.0% for single-line customers.
New customers (tenure <= 6 months) make up 21.0% of the base but churn at 52.9%, making onboarding quality a top retention priority.
55.0% of all customers are on flexible month-to-month contracts, representing the largest pool of at-risk revenue the business could convert to longer terms.
Streaming TV subscribers churn at 30.1% vs 33.5% for non-subscribers — entertainment add-ons show a modest retention benefit.
Online Backup subscribers churn at 21.5% vs 39.9% without it, another strong candidate for bundled retention offers.
Electronic check users represent 33.6% of customers but contribute disproportionately to churn — migrating them to autopay is a quick-win retention tactic.

A defined high-risk segment (month-to-month + tenure <=12mo + electronic check) contains 954 customers with a churn rate of 63.1%, nearly 2.4x the overall average — the top priority for a targeted win-back campaign.
Two-year contract customers retain at 97.2%, showing that contract length remains the single most effective retention lever available to the business.
Churned customers previously represented $139,130.85 in monthly billings — recovering even 20% of this segment would add roughly $27,826.17/month back to recurring revenue.

Cohort analysis shows retention has structurally weakened over time: the 2018Q1 acquisition cohort retains at 96.5%, while the 2023Q4 cohort (n=1,051) retains at just 43.2% — a clear downward trend in cohort quality/retention that predates any single recent event.

The best-performing acquisition cohort with a meaningful sample size (2018Q1, n=651) retains at 96.5%, showing the business has previously achieved much stronger retention than its current average — proof the churn rate isn't fixed.
The average customer lifetime among churned customers is just 17.98 months, underscoring how little time the business typically has to prove value before losing a customer.
Estimated Customer Lifetime Value varies more than 4x by contract type: two-year contract customers carry an estimated CLV of $3,723.45 versus just $930.70 for month-to-month customers.
Month-to-month customers have both the lowest average lifetime (14.0 months) and the highest churn rate (42.7%) of any contract segment, compounding their revenue disadvantage.
Two-year contract customers live over 4.4x longer on average than month-to-month customers, despite paying a lower average monthly charge — contract length drives lifetime revenue more than price.

The tenure-based churn curve peaks sharply in the first few months of service and decays steadily thereafter, confirming that onboarding-period intervention has the highest leverage per dollar spent on retention.

A rule-based risk-scoring model (contract + tenure + payment method + service add-ons) cleanly separates customers into four tiers: 'Very High Risk' customers churn at 65.2%, vs just 2.5% for 'Low Risk' customers — a 25.6x spread that validates the score as a targeting tool for retention campaigns.
'Very High Risk' customers alone represent $117,240.80 in monthly billings across 1,528 customers — the single highest-value target list for a proactive retention team.
